analysis.one_liner: Strengthens penalties and enforcement tools for women paid less than men for equal work.
analysis.headline: With 111 House cosponsors, the Paycheck Fairness Act never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Education and Workforce Committee's subcommittees until the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Equal Pay Act so women who are paid less than men for equal work can recover compensatory and punitive damages, join class actions, and are protected from retaliation for asking about or sharing wage information. It would also require federal agencies to collect and publish pay data by sex, train investigators, fund salary-negotiation training for women, and reward employers that voluntarily audit their pay scales. It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to two subcommittees, where it stayed until the Congress expired.
analysis.who_benefits: Working women who are underpaid relative to male colleagues, and their families, who currently can recover only back pay with no compensatory or punitive damages under the Equal Pay Act. Job applicants, people who want to discuss wages without fear of firing, and organizations that would run negotiation-skills training for girls and women also benefit.

how_it_helps.text: Adds compensatory and punitive damages for equal pay violations, which today allow recovery of back pay only, so victims of wage discrimination would have a remedy that actually deters employers [S2][S3].
Prohibits employers from retaliating against employees who inquire about, discuss, or disclose wages — the information workers need to discover pay discrimination in the first place [S3].
Allows equal pay claims to proceed as class actions and narrows employers' defense to only job-related, business-necessary factors, closing loopholes that make cases hard to win [S3].

Directs the EEOC to collect pay data by sex, race, and national origin and directs the Bureau of Labor Statistics and contract-compliance investigators to rebuild pay-equity data collection and enforcement methods [S2][S3].
Authorizes grants for salary-negotiation skills training for girls and women and creates voluntary employer guidelines, technical assistance, and a National Award for Pay Equity [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay women less than men for comparable work would face damages awards, class action exposure, new pay-data reporting, and closer federal contract-compliance investigations. Businesses that pay fairly would bear only new reporting paperwork.

drawbacks.text: The bill would expose employers to punitive damages and open-ended class actions over pay practices, raising litigation costs even for employers acting in good faith, since a payroll difference can exist without any discriminatory intent [S3].

It narrows the employer's defense: a pay difference based on education, training, or experience counts only if the employer proves it is job-related and shows no cheaper alternative practice exists, shifting the burden of proof onto businesses and requiring them to justify ordinary pay decisions [S3].
Removing the 'within any establishment' limit means wages could be compared across an employer's different facilities, making it harder for employers to defend regional pay differences [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The Equal Pay Act's remedies have long been considered weak — back pay only, no damages for emotional or financial harm, no class actions — so pay discrimination largely carries no penalty. This bill fixes that squarely, and the main cost is litigation and compliance exposure for employers, some of it unavoidable and some of it genuine friction for businesses that pay fairly. On balance the public benefit of enforceable equal pay outweighs the burden, though the damages and burden-of-proof changes would have drawn legitimate employer objections in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, then to two of its subcommittees, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the Paycheck Fairness Act on April 19, 2005 with an initial group of cosponsors [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce that same day [S5].
On May 9, 2005 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations and the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections [S5].
Ultimately 111 House members — all Democrats — cosponsored the bill, and no further action of any kind was taken before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced compensatory and punitive damages, class actions, and new pay-data reporting are better off because the bill never advanced; women facing pay discrimination are left with the unchanged, weaker remedies of the Equal Pay Act.

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.role: Sponsor, House Education and Workforce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 60 original cosponsors from across the House Democratic caucus [S1][S3].

for.name: 111 of 201 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 111 cosponsors were Democrats [S4].

against.name: Rep. John Boehner
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or hearing for the bill, which stayed in subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to two subcommittees on May 9, 2005 and took no further action on it [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 111 cosponsors were House Democrats, and the bill never moved in a committee chaired by a Republican; there were no votes on the bill, so no formal partisan split was ever recorded [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Employers with pay gaps between male and female workers
industries.note: The bill would let underpaid workers recover compensatory and punitive damages, sue as a class, and compare wages across facilities, and would require new pay-data reporting — a direct financial cost for employers whose pay scales disadvantage women. Its interest in blocking the bill ran against workers seeking to be paid equally for equal work.

Contract-compliance investigators would be directed to use a full range of investigative methods, survey at least half of nonconstruction contractor establishments each year, and collect pay data by sex, race, and national origin — closer scrutiny of federal contractors' compensation practices.
